title: Incomplete examination after postoperative voice change

cues.phrase: gagging ended the examination when the tip was above the epiglottis
cues.why: The explicitly aborted examination advertises an unfinished task. Completing the scope becomes an obvious next action before the learner needs to analyze the recorded anatomy. This is a partial completion cue, not a diagnosis disclosure; it does not by itself distinguish every offered modality.

fairness: Awake flexible laryngoscopy is the best offered next examination for persistent post-thyroidectomy dysphonia with possible aspiration when fold movement has not been documented. The swallow study is clinically relevant but does not replace evaluating the vocal folds. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

The added prior-scope history does not create a second consequential inference as written. Removing it still leaves persistent postoperative voice change requiring laryngeal visualization; saying the examination ended early supplies its inadequacy rather than leaving a competing interpretation to resolve. CT is a weak competitor without an established unexplained paralysis or other structural question. This remains a high-yield first-assessment rule.

The four-week chronology, age, sex and symptoms are clear. The standalone task does not depend on another node. Gagging during an earlier attempt does not itself make a repeat awake flexible examination inappropriate.
suggestions: Use a clinically supported prior report that appears reassuring but whose actual observation or task coverage must be interpreted, and make that interpretation change the next examination. Avoid merely announcing an aborted examination. Preserve the voice and aspiration findings.

Offer plausible examinations for the residual uncertainty at the same stage. If no genuine competing interpretation can be supplied, seek explicit acceptance as foundational postoperative assessment rather than claiming difficult two-step reasoning.

title: Cross-sectional mapping when invasive thyroid cancer is suspected

The resident must infer possible deep/invasive disease and then weigh useful contrast-enhanced anatomy against a possible later radioiodine course. Noncontrast CT is a credible iodine-avoidance error; the two CT labels are parallel. Mentioning radioiodine introduces a real competing consideration rather than announcing that contrast is permissible.

The known papillary diagnosis appropriately precedes a different management task. Renal function and the absence of an acute airway problem support the proposed elective assessment. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified; this review does not establish a particular postcontrast radioiodine interval.
This is a complete standalone case. It does not require the earlier mapping or later nodal-surgery task to supply the cancer diagnosis, imaging findings or current decision.

fairness: Right thyroid lobectomy is the strongest offered treatment. The resident must distinguish successful biochemical control from unresolved mechanical disease, then choose treatment extent using the contralateral evidence. The preference for definitive treatment does not uniquely select lobectomy because all three options propose definitive treatment. The contralateral workup is necessary to the extent decision.
